lead: Hyperledger is an open-source family of permissioned blockchain frameworks. It exists because enterprises need shared ledgers with known members, not anonymous miners. Hyperledger Fabric is the best known: a channel runs on peers, orderers and cryptographic identities, and a transaction commits only when an endorsement policy is met. Banks, exporters and insurers use this model when they must agree on records without exposing them to the public internet.
prereq: You need Unit 1's private and consortium blockchain types and Unit 3's transaction life cycle, plus 6.2 for the contract side.

blocks.text: Hyperledger is not one blockchain. It is an umbrella project hosted by the Linux Foundation. Common frameworks include Fabric for general enterprise ledgers, Sawtooth for modular transaction families, Indy for decentralized identity, Besu for Ethereum-compatible enterprise chains, and Iroha for small trusted networks. Each has a different design goal, so the names are not synonyms.
Two tools sit around the frameworks. Explorer reads a ledger and shows blocks and transactions. Caliper measures throughput and latency, so a team can compare a chaincode change with a baseline.
The building blocks are the same ideas under different names. Some syllabi call them components.

items: Ledger: the append-only block history plus the current world state.
Membership: who may join and what each identity may do.

Consensus: how nodes agree on order. Fabric uses Raft for ordering. Earlier releases offered a Kafka-based ordering service for production networks and a single-node Solo orderer for development and testing only; both are now deprecated. Names only here; proofs are in Unit 3.
Chaincode: the smart contract that reads and writes state. See 6.2.
Events: notifications that let an outside application react after a commit.

blocks.text: Fabric assumes members are known. An organisation is a company or authority with its own membership service provider (MSP). The MSP turns certificates into roles: a peer identity, an admin identity, a client identity. A user cannot simply invent a key and write; the channel checks the MSP.

A peer hosts a copy of the ledger and runs chaincode. A peer can be an endorser, a committer, or both. An orderer receives endorsed transactions, puts them in a block, and delivers the block to peers. The orderer does not run chaincode and does not execute business logic. That is the commonest exam confusion.

A channel is a private subnet of the same Fabric network. Only organisations joined to the channel see its ledger. Two firms can share a channel for invoices while a regulator joins a separate audit channel. Channels give privacy by separation, not by encryption of one global ledger.

Private data goes further. A chaincode can keep a data collection off-chain and write only a hash to the channel ledger. Members of the collection see the raw value; other channel members see the hash and can later verify that the value was not changed.

items: A client sends a proposal to the peers named by the endorsement policy.
Each peer simulates chaincode against its copy of state, signs a read-write set, and returns an endorsement.
The client collects endorsements and sends them to the orderer.
The orderer orders transactions into a block; it does not validate business rules.

Committer peers check signatures, the endorsement policy, and read-set versions. A version change means another transaction already wrote that key. The earlier transaction stays valid; the transaction now being validated is marked invalid and is not applied to world state.
Valid transactions update world state and append to the ledger; events fire.

blocks.text: An endorsement policy is a rule over MSP identities, for example "1 of Org A AND 1 of Org B". Extra signatures are allowed but not required. A transaction can be endorsed and still fail commit if its read-set version is stale.

This split keeps ordering simple and keeps execution with the members who own the data. It is why Fabric is called an execute-order-validate architecture, unlike the order-execute design of public chains. See 6.8 for the throughput cost of this trade.

figure.caption: A client collects endorsements from the peers named by the policy, the orderer places the transaction in a block, and a committer validates it before writing the channel ledger.

spec.title: Fabric transaction flow
spec.aria: A client sends a proposal to two peers, both endorse, the orderer orders a block, a committer validates it, and the channel ledger is written.

examples.question: Org A has peers A1 and A2. Org B has peers B1 and B2. One orderer serves the channel. The endorsement policy is "1 of Org A AND 1 of Org B". A proposal is endorsed by A1, A2 and B1. (a) How many distinct organisations endorsed? (b) How many endorsements came from Org A? (c) Does the set satisfy the policy?
steps: List the endorsers: A1, A2, B1.
Map each peer to its organisation: A1 → Org A, A2 → Org A, B1 → Org B.
Distinct organisations = {Org A, Org B}, so the count is 2.
Endorsements from Org A = A1 and A2, so the count is 2.
Policy needs at least one from Org A and at least one from Org B. Org A is present and Org B is present, so the policy is satisfied.
The extra Org A signature (A2) is allowed; the policy does not forbid extra endorsements.
examples.answer: Two distinct organisations endorsed, Org A supplied two endorsements, and the AND policy is satisfied; the extra A2 signature is allowed.
examples.check:
peers_A = ["A1", "A2"]
peers_B = ["B1", "B2"]
endorsers = ["A1", "A2", "B1"]
orgs = set()
for e in endorsers:
    if e in peers_A:
        orgs.add("A")
    elif e in peers_B:
        orgs.add("B")
print(len(orgs))
print(sum(1 for e in endorsers if e in peers_A))
print(1 if ("A" in orgs and "B" in orgs) else 0)

traps: Calling the orderer a miner. A Fabric orderer orders transactions into blocks; it does not execute chaincode or mine.
Treating a channel as an organisation. One organisation can join many channels, and one channel can serve several organisations.
Confusing endorsement with commit. A transaction can collect valid endorsements and still be invalidated at commit by a read-set version mismatch.
Treating an MSP identity as a website login. The MSP is a certificate-backed membership record checked by the channel.
Assuming private data is fully hidden by the hash. The hash proves integrity; only collection members receive the raw value.

quiz.a: Fabric, Sawtooth, Indy, Besu and Iroha.

quiz.q: Why does Fabric use channels instead of one global ledger?
quiz.a: A channel gives a private ledger to the organisations joined to it. Other organisations do not see that channel's transactions, so privacy comes from separation rather than from encrypting a single shared ledger.

quiz.q: A channel policy is "1 of Org A AND 1 of Org B". Endorsers are A1, B1 and B2. Does the set satisfy the policy?
quiz.a: Yes. Org A is present through A1, and Org B is present through B1 and B2. At least one from each organisation satisfies the AND policy.

quiz.q: An orderer receives 100 endorsed transactions. Explain what it does and what it does not do.
quiz.a: It orders the transactions into a block and delivers that block to committer peers. It does not run chaincode, check business rules, or execute the endorsement policy; those checks happen at endorsement and at commit.
Chaincode is the smart contract that runs on peers, reads and writes channel state, and is simulated during endorsement. More in 6.2.

quiz.q: State the difference between a peer and an orderer.
quiz.a: A peer hosts the ledger and runs chaincode; it can endorse and commit. An orderer receives endorsed transactions, puts them in order inside blocks, and delivers blocks to peers. The orderer does not execute chaincode.

quiz.q: A committer finds that a transaction's read-set version no longer matches world state. What happens to that transaction?
quiz.a: The transaction is marked invalid. It is not applied to world state, even though it may have valid endorsements. The block is still appended to the ledger history.

quiz.q: Why can a private data collection store only a hash on the channel ledger?
quiz.a: The raw value stays with collection members. The hash on the ledger lets any later reader verify that the value was not changed. Non-members see the hash but not the value, so confidentiality and integrity are separated.

beyond: Not for the exam. Fabric is used in trade finance, food traceability and central-bank pilots. Newer curricula add Fabric Gateway, chaincode-as-a-service and Kubernetes deployment. Search "Fabric endorsement policy", "Fabric private data" and "Hyperledger Caliper benchmark" for the next layer.
